title: India confirms Bangladesh consular talks put off as Hasina passport row deepens
dek: India's foreign ministry confirmed on Friday that the first formal talks in more than two years on visas, detainees and the border are off for now, and called extradition "a legal matter" as the row over Sheikh Hasina's passport deepens.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The first formal talks between India and Bangladesh on visas, detained citizens and border management in more than two years will not take place next week as planned, according to reports, after a row over former prime minister Sheikh Hasina's request for a new Bangladeshi passport deepened the strain between the two governments.

The fifth round of the India-Bangladesh Consular Dialogue had been scheduled for 17 and 18 November in Dhaka. Reports on Thursday, citing unnamed diplomatic sources in Dhaka and New Delhi, said the meeting had been postponed, and on Friday evening India's Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) confirmed it. Its spokesperson, Randhir Jaiswal, said the meeting would be held "on a mutually convenient date" but gave neither a reason nor a new date.

## What India said on Friday

At the MEA's weekly briefing on Friday, Mr Jaiswal said: "India desires a positive, constructive and forward-looking relationship with Bangladesh." He said India remained ready to discuss all bilateral issues through existing mechanisms, "including at the technical level", in areas such as trade, railways, water resources and border management, and that the postponed round would also take up the renewal of the travel arrangement between the two countries, according to reports of the briefing.

Asked about Ms Hasina, he said: "Extradition is a legal matter and it will be dealt with accordingly." Pressed on her plan to return to Bangladesh in December, he said: "When I talked about the legal matter, it is about the extradition part of it. To the other part of your question, I have no comment to offer." He also declined to comment on reports about how she might travel and on whether she would receive a fair trial, according to reports.

In Dhaka, Khairul Kabir Khokon, a joint secretary general of the governing Bangladesh Nationalist Party, called her passport request an attempt "to create instability", in an interview reported on Friday. Inside Bangladesh, police continued a crackdown on the banned Awami League: Dhaka police said 15 members of a banned organisation were arrested on Friday while trying to hold marches at four places in the city, and police in the Chattogram range said 1,210 people had been arrested across 11 districts in 24 hours on Thursday, 131 of them Awami League members, according to reports.

## What happened

The dialogue, a director-general-level meeting set up in 2017, was to be led by Esha Srivastava, joint secretary in charge of the MEA's consular, passport and visa division, and Shah Asif Rahman, director general of the South Asia wing of Bangladesh's foreign ministry, according to reports from late October. Four rounds have been held so far, the most recent in New Delhi on 29 May 2024, weeks before the uprising that ended Ms Hasina's 15 years in power.

Bangladesh had proposed holding it in late October; India asked for November because of Durga Puja, reports said. The agreed agenda covered border management, visa services, the repatriation of detained nationals, the release of fishermen held by each side, a Mutual Legal Assistance Treaty, and renewal of a travel arrangement that has been extended every six months since it lapsed in 2023. India's priority was fishermen: an official at the Indian High Commission in Dhaka said New Delhi had shared a draft protocol to speed up their return, according to reports.

Dhaka had also said it would use the meeting to raise the extradition of Ms Hasina and of her former home minister Asaduzzaman Khan Kamal. "Dhaka will seek the extradition of political figures currently taking refuge in India," an unnamed Bangladeshi foreign ministry official said on 30 October, according to reports. It would have been the first time Bangladesh raised the demand at a formal bilateral meeting since August 2024. Reports differ on whether extradition was on the agreed agenda or only on Dhaka's list.

## The passport row

On 9 November a London law firm, Matrix Chambers, wrote on Ms Hasina's behalf to Bangladesh's acting high commissioner in New Delhi, Preeti Rahman, asking for a new passport and national identity card. The letter said both had been cancelled by the former interim government and other authorities, and that she planned to return to Bangladesh and surrender to a court in December, on a date still to be announced, according to reports.

Bangladesh's government rejected the request the same day. "Bangladesh does not issue passports to terrorists. We have asked for them to be handed over," the State Minister for Foreign Affairs, Humaiun Kobir, told journalists at the foreign ministry. He called the application "utterly ridiculous", said the mission could not verify the firm's authority to act for her, and said she could come back only by being handed over under the extradition treaty, surrendering to a court and serving her sentence.

At a meeting of the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party's parliamentary party on 9 November, chaired by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said the government would act under the existing extradition treaty if she tried to return, according to MPs present, reports said.

Before Friday, India's position had been guarded: on 10 November Mr Jaiswal said only that any extradition request would be handled "through the appropriate legal process".

## Background

Ms Hasina fled to India on 5 August 2024 as a student-led uprising swept her government from power, and has lived there since. Bangladesh's International Crimes Tribunal sentenced her in absentia in November 2025 to death on one charge and life imprisonment on another, for crimes against humanity during the crackdown on the protests. She denies the charges. Dhaka first asked for her extradition by diplomatic note in December 2024, and renewed the request after the verdict. India has acknowledged receiving the requests but has not said whether it will act on them, according to reports.

The two countries signed an extradition treaty in 2013, which was amended in 2016.

The row comes during a tense period inside Bangladesh. Since 7 November, police have blamed the banned Awami League for a wave of bus burnings and crude-bomb blasts; the party has not formally responded. And the 1996 treaty under which India and Bangladesh share the Ganga's waters at Farakka expires on 12 December, with no replacement yet announced.

## Why it matters for India and Bengal

The consular dialogue is the main working channel for problems that touch ordinary people on both sides of a 4,096-km border, more than half of it in West Bengal: visas for patients, students and traders, the return of people detained for crossing without papers, and fishermen held by the other country's coast guard. A delay leaves those cases where they are. Bangladesh's list for the meeting also included what it calls push-ins, people it says are sent across the border from India, an issue that plays out along the West Bengal frontier.

For New Delhi, the passport row narrows the room it has had to keep Ms Hasina's status vague. If she tries to travel in December, India will have to decide whether to let her leave without a valid Bangladeshi document, hand her over, or keep her, and each choice carries costs for its relations with a government in Dhaka that it has been trying to rebuild ties with since the BNP took office.

## What happens next

- 16-18 November: Prime Minister Narendra Modi is in Manila for the ASEAN-India and East Asia summits; Bangladesh is not an ASEAN member.
- A new date for the consular dialogue has not been announced; the MEA says it will be held on a mutually convenient date.
- December: Ms Hasina has said she will return to Bangladesh and surrender to a court; no date has been given.
- 12 December: the Ganga Water Treaty expires.
